I really like these friendslop games but this one doesn't hit well enough with its gimmick. RV There Yet has the vehicles, REPO has its wacky physics. I thought it would have been VR, but I don't think it took advantage of the medium as well as it could have. This feels like a smaller scale Lethal Company with some buggy object physicality put on the side. It feels unpolished and there's nothing new or innovative with their approach. Secondly it's obviously designed as a VR Quest title first. This isn't a problem on its own but it just means that its target demographic is definitely on the more... younger side. PC lobbies could be implemented to help, but I understand why they might not want to do that. It's just an unfavourable experience to jump into as a PCVR user. YOU'LL NEED TO CONVINCE YOUR FREINDS TO PURCHASE THIS WITH YOU. There is still some potential for the game to improve but if you were hoping for a thrilling and dynamic co-op horror VR experience, this isn't really it. It's all very predictable. Some might be okay with it though, which is why I was on the fence for my rating. But based on what I played this personally was not the VR co-op thriller that I was anticipating and that I know is possible.

It's got a solid foundation as a co-op VR game, essentially being a VR rendition of REPO or Lethal Company where you bring the valuables into the dungeon instead of taking them out. Just one major flaw that kills it all for me is the level generation. Far too often does a level generate in a way where one large monster completely roadblocks the only path, forcing you to dip out as the only alternative is dying. If this were more avoidable, then the game would be plenty of fun with friends.

Deadly Delivery is a chaotic cooperative VR horror game that turns a simple delivery job into a constant cycle of panic, laughter, teamwork, and disaster. Developed by Flat Head Studio and published alongside Creature Label, the game combines physics-based gameplay, proximity voice chat, monster survival, and multiplayer cooperation into an experience that feels uniquely suited for virtual reality. While many horror co-op games focus heavily on atmosphere or pure survival mechanics, Deadly Delivery succeeds because it understands how naturally funny and terrifying VR becomes when players are forced to physically interact with dangerous environments under pressure. The premise is wonderfully absurd. Players become goblin-like delivery workers tasked with transporting valuable cargo through dark mines and underground tunnels filled with supernatural threats. Every mission revolves around moving heavy packages across unstable terrain while avoiding deadly creatures hidden throughout the caves. What makes the gameplay so entertaining is how quickly simple tasks become chaotic once monsters appear or teammates begin panicking. Carrying a fragile box across a collapsing bridge while someone screams over voice chat about a creature approaching creates the exact kind of unpredictable multiplayer chaos that VR handles exceptionally well. The physical interaction systems are easily the strongest part of the game. Deadly Delivery fully embraces VR mechanics by making nearly every action require direct movement and interaction. Players climb ladders manually, carry heavy cargo with both hands, use flashlights and radios physically, and interact with equipment in ways that make the world feel tangible. The physics intentionally feel somewhat clumsy, which creates countless hilarious situations where teammates accidentally drop boxes, crash carts into walls, or stumble into danger while trying to escape monsters. Instead of feeling frustrating most of the time, these mistakes become part of the game’s identity and generate some of its funniest moments. The horror elements are surprisingly effective despite the game’s comedic tone. The mines are filled with disturbing creatures that constantly pressure players while exploring deeper into dangerous areas. Some enemies stalk players silently while others create psychological tension by mimicking voices or forcing teams to separate in darkness. The proximity voice chat system plays a huge role in the atmosphere because hearing distant screams or uncertain calls for help through echoing tunnels becomes genuinely unsettling. There are moments where players hesitate before responding to teammates because they are no longer sure whether the voice belongs to a friend or something pretending to be one. One of the game’s biggest strengths is how naturally it balances horror and comedy. The cartoon-inspired visuals and exaggerated physics prevent the experience from becoming oppressively dark, but the tension still remains high during dangerous encounters. The game constantly creates situations where fear immediately turns into laughter. A carefully planned mission can collapse instantly because someone accidentally drops critical supplies into a pit or attracts a monster while panicking. These unpredictable moments are what make Deadly Delivery so memorable during multiplayer sessions. Progression systems help give the game long-term replayability beyond the initial novelty. Completing successful deliveries rewards players with currency that can be spent on new equipment, tools, cosmetics, pets, and utility upgrades. Better flashlights, scanners, carrying tools, and survival gear gradually make later missions more manageable while encouraging players to specialize in different roles during team runs. Some players naturally become scouts while others focus on carrying cargo, protecting teammates, or navigating dangerous terrain. This light progression system gives the gameplay enough structure to keep players invested over multiple sessions. Visually, the game performs impressively well for an indie VR title. The stylized comic-book-inspired art direction gives environments and monsters strong personality while maintaining clear visibility during chaotic situations. Lighting is especially important because much of the tension comes from navigating dark tunnels with limited visibility. Flashlights, glowing hazards, and dim environmental lighting all contribute heavily to the oppressive atmosphere. The visual style also helps soften the horror enough that players who normally avoid intense horror games can still enjoy the experience. The audio design deserves a great deal of praise as well. Creature noises, environmental effects, distant echoes, and panicked voice chat interactions constantly reinforce immersion. The soundscape makes the caves feel alive and dangerous even during quieter moments. Hearing teammates slowly disappear into darkness while their voices fade into static or screams creates tension that few non-VR horror games can replicate effectively. However, the game is heavily dependent on multiplayer to truly shine. Playing with friends creates a fantastic experience filled with emergent storytelling and constant chaos, but solo play feels significantly weaker. Without the unpredictable social interaction and shared panic, the gameplay loop becomes more repetitive and less exciting. Public matchmaking helps somewhat, but random groups rarely capture the same energy and chemistry as playing with a coordinated group of friends. The physics systems, while entertaining, can occasionally become frustrating as well. Awkward collisions, accidental item drops, or unpredictable movement sometimes lead to deaths that feel unfair rather than funny. Certain missions can spiral into disaster almost immediately due to unlucky monster placement or environmental hazards, creating inconsistent difficulty between runs. Some players will enjoy this unpredictability, while others may find the randomness occasionally irritating. Mission variety is another area where the game could improve over time. Although procedural generation helps keep maps unpredictable, the core structure of transporting packages through dangerous environments eventually becomes repetitive during extended play sessions. The game relies heavily on emergent multiplayer interactions to maintain freshness, which means enjoyment often depends on the quality of the group playing together. Despite these flaws, Deadly Delivery succeeds because it fully understands what makes cooperative VR games memorable. The physical interaction, chaotic teamwork, horror atmosphere, and unpredictable disasters combine into an experience that naturally creates hilarious and tense stories players want to share afterward. Every failed mission feels entertaining because something ridiculous almost always happens before everything falls apart completely. For VR players looking for a cooperative horror game built around teamwork, panic, and comedy, Deadly Delivery is one of the most enjoyable multiplayer experiences currently available. It may not be the deepest or most polished VR game on the market, but its creativity, atmosphere, and constant multiplayer chaos make it incredibly difficult to stop playing with the right group of friends. Rating: 9/10

Me and a few friends have put a fair amount of hours into this game, but it's so difficult to put even more into it considering its current state. It shows a lot of promise, but the developers are not fixing game breaking bugs that ruin the game completely for everyone. The game is an absolute buggy mess at the moment. Every single session, you will run into multiple game breaking bugs, and from looking at the past few updates, these aren't being addressed and instead more content/cosmetics is being prioritised. One of the worst bugs involves purchasing a pet, and then the pet not following you because someone picked it up even for a split second. As soon as any other player other than the owner of the pet picks it up, it will sit still and never move again until the owner goes back for it and picks it up themselves. Items randomly disappear when you die for some unknown reason (this happens very often), even if you check every single corner of the room after you've died and dropped your items. Sometimes when you place a package on a doorstep securely and ring the bell, the package doesn't get taken, you don't earn any money and the door shuts off completely as if a package was delivered. Sometimes when your squad is wiped or you run out of time and nobody is at base, you lose your pet completely. The whole point of the pets is to have more storage and for it to carry over if you die/fail, so one of the major selling points for the pets is completely irrelevant half of the time. What makes this even worse is that the game will still think you have a pet, and will not let you purchase another one. With the newest update another two annoying bugs have been introduced: Sometimes other players (outside of the host) can't purchase items unless the host switches the page to the correct one in the shop. Other players can still switch between the five pages in the shop, but can't purchase items half the time if the host hasn't switched pages as well. Putting any package into your pockets, a pet or a bag will misalign the package completely so that it is floating outside of the zone it is meant to be in. This seems to happen incredibly frequently, each time we buy a bag and put anything in it, it randomly causes all the packages to start floating around the bag or much further away from it which makes it really difficult to try move them around or pick the correct one. If the developers actually prioritise fixing game breaking bugs instead of adding new content and cosmetics, this can be an excellent game. The vibe and general gameplay is great! But all of the bugs mentioned above (and many other minor ones) are ruining the game really badly right now. You never have a session of this game without running into multiple game breaking bugs. It is unlikely me and my friends will be continuing with this game for the time being unless the game becomes more stable, and it's really hard to recommend this to anyone with how riddled with bugs it currently is.
